capabilities.target: Chat reply to the authenticated requester
Arbitrary public web page by URL
Jira tickets, including tickets filed by customers

inputs.source: Employee question submitted via SSO-authenticated chat
Content of engineering design docs returned by docs.search
Content fetched via the planned web.fetch tool
Tickets filed by customers, retrieved via the planned Jira MCP server

instructions.note: The instruction does not limit which documents are in scope or restrict results by the requester's role; any confidential design doc docs.search returns may be surfaced to any authenticated employee.

The only stated safeguard against leaking sensitive content is a behavioral instruction ('never paste secrets or credentials'). It is the sole control in this position, does not cover confidential content generally, and was not written with the planned web.fetch egress tool in mind.

elements.name: Jira MCP server / customer ticket submitters

controls.name: Chat client does not render images or fetch links
Only engineers can write to design docs
Agent cannot modify its own configuration
Prompt rule: never paste secrets or credentials
controls.decay_rationale: A more capable or indirectly-injected model may still comply literally with 'never paste secrets' while paraphrasing, summarizing, or encoding other confidential content; it does not cover general confidential disclosure and was not written with a future egress tool in mind. Weakens under model_upgrade and longer_task_horizon.

controls.name: Prompt rule: answer using docs.search and cite the document
controls.decay_rationale: A citation instruction does not prevent inclusion of confidential content in the answer and offers no resistance to an adversarial instruction override as model capability grows.

controls.name: Human approval gate on web.fetch calls following a docs.search read
Injection classifier / trust tagging on Jira and web content
controls.decay_rationale: The classifier sees content, not intent; multi-turn or multi-document injection payloads can still get past it. Weakens under model_upgrade, new_mcp_server, and data_scope_expansion.

controls.name: Pin and verify Jira MCP server and tool definitions
Tamper-evident log of docs.search and web.fetch invocations

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1) activates once the planned web.fetch tool and Jira customer-ticket MCP server ship

attack_path.note: A customer-filed Jira ticket (or fetched web page, in.web_content) carries attacker-authored instructions once the planned MCP server or tool exist.
The injected instructions direct the agent to retrieve confidential engineering design docs.
The injected instructions direct the agent to call the planned web.fetch tool with the confidential content embedded in the request URL, exfiltrating it to an attacker-controlled destination.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Tool manifest or MCP client config diff showing a web.fetch tool or a Jira MCP server added; the roadmap item shipping to production.

evidence.observation: Next sprint adds a web.fetch tool so answers can include public references, and a Jira MCP server that includes tickets filed by customers; neither is built yet.
Design docs are confidential and readable via cap.docs_search; once web.fetch exists, their content could be embedded in an outbound request URL.
The only stated safeguard is a behavioral instruction not to paste secrets or credentials; it does not mention confidential design content generally and was not written with an egress tool in mind.
There is no network egress today and the docs credential is read only, which is why the complete attack path does not exist yet.

recommendations.action: Before enabling web.fetch, add a destination allowlist that pins fetch targets to a fixed set of reference domains and strips any model- or document-derived text from the request, so the sink stays unreachable for arbitrary attacker destinations rather than merely harder to reach.
Require raw-action human approval, showing the literal URL and arguments, before any web.fetch call that follows a docs.search read in the same turn.
Tag content retrieved from the Jira MCP server and from web.fetch as untrusted and run it through an injection classifier before it can influence tool selection.
Pin and hash Jira MCP tool and server definitions before connecting, and verify server identity.
Log every docs.search and web.fetch invocation with the authenticated requester identity and the destination URL in a tamper-evident store.

stride_coverage.rationale: No external protocol peers or agent cards exist in the present design for an attacker to spoof; the requester's identity is established by SSO before the chat reaches the agent.
autonomy.can_modify_own_config is false and no capability lets the agent alter its own prompt or configuration.
No audit log ties docs.search or the planned web.fetch invocations to a tamper-evident record; this absence compounds the exfiltration risk once egress exists.
Once web.fetch and the Jira MCP server exist, confidential design doc content read via docs.search could be embedded in an outbound fetch request.
Artifacts do not state whether a rate limit, spend cap, or step limit bounds docs.search or the planned web.fetch and Jira calls.

Once web.fetch exists, injected instructions could cause the agent to perform an outbound action on data no ordinary requester could send externally themselves, a confused-deputy style privilege gain.
SSO authentication verifies the requester's identity before any question reaches the agent.
SSO establishes identity at authentication time, but artifacts do not state whether individual questions and answers are logged against that identity.
Only engineers can write to the design docs store per the runtime notes.
Artifacts do not describe the design docs store's own read access control list beyond stating the docs are confidential.
A document store read by a single low-volume internal Q&A agent is not a meaningful denial-of-service target in this design.
Any destination reachable by an unrestricted web.fetch can present itself as a legitimate reference source while actually being an attacker-controlled exfiltration endpoint.
No record would tie a given web.fetch request to the instruction that triggered it.
Any customer who can file a ticket can author content the agent treats as task-relevant, without the ticket's instructions being distinguishable from legitimate internal direction.
No stated mechanism attributes agent actions back to the specific ticket content that triggered them.
The content and destination of a web.fetch call can be shaped by upstream injected instructions, tampering with the agent's intended action.
This outbound flow is the egress channel through which confidential design doc content could leave the trust boundary.
Artifacts do not state whether the planned web.fetch tool would have a timeout, size limit, or rate limit.
Fetched web content is untrusted and could carry injected instructions that redirect the agent's subsequent tool calls.
This inbound flow carries fetched content into the agent's context; it does not itself move internal data outward.
No stated limit on the size or number of pages web.fetch could retrieve per query.
Customer-filed ticket content is untrusted and could carry injected instructions that redirect the agent's subsequent tool calls, a classic indirect prompt injection vector.
This inbound flow carries ticket content into the agent's context; it does not itself move internal data outward.
No stated limit on the number or size of Jira tickets ingested per query via the planned MCP server.

rating.rationale: No finding has horizon:present above low: the current design has no egress-capable capability, so no untrusted source can reach a sensitive sink today (rubric 5a). The single finding, a lethal trifecta (TC1), is horizon:forecast because it depends entirely on two roadmap items -- a web.fetch tool and a Jira MCP server that ingests customer-filed tickets -- that are not built yet. Once either new_tool or new_mcp_server fires, the design has no structural control covering the resulting read-then-egress path (the only declared controls either don't exist yet, cover a different capability, or are weak, dependent prompt instructions), so the projected tier is critical. The single control whose removal drives this forecast is the current absence of any network-egress-capable tool (ctrl.no_egress_capability); adding web.fetch directly eliminates it.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in prompt.md and the runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.

No MCP configuration, tool manifest, or IaC was provided for the current state; capability scope for docs.search and the chat client is inferred from the runtime notes, so confidence on present-day scope is medium.

The web.fetch tool and Jira MCP server are described only as roadmap items with no design detail (authentication, credential scope, URL construction, rate limits); the forecast finding's projected tier assumes a typical, uncontrolled implementation of each and should be re-assessed against the actual implementation before it ships.
No information was provided about logging, audit trail, or rate/spend limits for the current agent; the related STRIDE categories are marked not_assessed rather than scored.
